summary: This Smile Generation article explains how to tell whether a tooth extraction is healing properly, covering the first 24 hours and the days, weeks and months afterward. It stresses protecting the blood clot to avoid dry socket, with rest, soft foods, no straws or spitting, and gentle rinsing. It also notes that dentists extract teeth for decay, crowding or impacted wisdom teeth, and points readers to the Find A Dentist tool.
one_line: A Smile Generation guide to tooth extraction healing stages, aftercare dos and don'ts, and dry socket warning signs.
key_facts: A dentist may pull a tooth for tooth decay, crowding, or an impacted wisdom tooth.
Most of the care and attention during recovery happens in the first three days, though full healing can take a few months.
Signs of concern in the first three days include active bleeding, pain after day three, and loss of the blood clot causing dry socket.
Dry socket is described as the most common complication from tooth extractions.
Patients should rest often with their head elevated, keeping the head upright or above the heart even when sleeping, to lessen bleeding.
Patients should avoid using a straw and avoid spitting, since these put pressure on the newly forming blood clot.
Patients should plan to be lying down for the first 24 hours after extraction.
During the first 48 hours patients should avoid rinsing with anything, including mouthwash, and avoid activity that raises the heart rate or causes straining.
At three days, patients may gently rinse with warm salt water or a medicated mouthwash, avoiding vigorous swishing and gurgling.
By one week, stitches are either removed or dissolved, and pain, bleeding, and swelling should have ceased except for some sensitivity.
At two weeks the site should be mostly healed, with tissue closing up instead of an open socket.
At three weeks and beyond, the site should have no pain, bleeding, or swelling, though it may stay sensitive a little longer.
The article is reviewed by Charles Rodgers, DDS, and was published Apr 01, 2022 and updated Nov 01, 2023.
The cited source for the article is the Mouth Healthy “Extractions” page dated 23 Feb. 2022.
